title: One officer, poised to understand
article: If ever there was a police officer perfectly positioned to understand Otto Vass, the mentally ill man who died after a violent struggle with Toronto police more than six years ago, it was Detective-Constable Phil Duncan.

He took the job with an unusual amount of relevant life experience: In high school, he volunteered with the mentally and physically disabled; at university, he was a few credits away from a psychology degree when family circumstances dictated that he return home and look after his mother, and for those two years or so, he also worked full time with the seriously mentally ill in group homes and a life skills centre.
"I was very comfortable [with those with psychiatric problems]" he said yesterday, "and cognizant of ways to interact with people suffering from these issues."
And Det.-Const. Duncan is such a gentle, soft-spoken fellow that if anyone could appear unthreatening and approachable in uniform, it might be him.
He was testifying at the coroner's inquest into Mr. Vass's sudden death in the early morning hours of Aug. 9, 2000, in the parking lot of a 7-Eleven in west-end Toronto.

Det.-Const. Duncan was the second of four Toronto officers to testify at the inquest, all of whom were once criminally charged with manslaughter in Mr. Vass's death, all of whom were acquitted after a jury trial, but who are nonetheless being questioned here by one lawyer, Peter Rosenthal, as though they were all liars who conspired to cover up the facts of Mr. Vass's death.

After trying unsuccessfully first to win standing as the lawyer for the Committee for Justice for Otto Vass (a collection of activists) and then to act for the committee on behalf of Mr. Vass's widow Zsuzsanna, who isn't up to attending the proceedings herself, Mr. Rosenthal was belatedly granted standing on behalf of Mr. Vass's son, Attila.

Mr. Rosenthal's view appears to be that for all the blah-blah-blah about inquests not being adversarial proceedings, the public interest requires that they ought to be. I don't disagree, but it should be noted that Mr. Rosenthal, by his presence, often ensures that they are unnecessarily so.

To judge by his questioning yesterday of Det.-Const. Duncan, and a report of his cross-examination of Det.-Const. Duncan's partner, Detective-Constable Robert Lemaitre, who testified last Friday, Mr. Rosenthal's theory is that the two officers used excessive force with Mr. Vass; that in his words, they ought to "have backed off" when without provocation, Mr. Vass punched Det.-Const. Lemaitre in the face, and that they then conspired, with two other officers who arrived as their backup, in a cover-up.
Indeed, Mr. Rosenthal last week outright accused Det.-Const. Lemaitre of being a "very dishonest witness" who was "making it up as he goes along."

With Det.-Const. Duncan, Mr. Rosenthal was only slightly less direct, once suggesting it "is inconceivable you are being honest" and at another that if he ever saw a fellow officer use too much force, he "would never ever report" but would fall into the "code of silence" that binds officers to one another.

"I disagree with you," Det.-Const. Duncan said, ever mild. "I joined this job - I have a lot of integrity - because I want to help people. Am I saying it (the code of silence) never happens? No. But I'd have no problem if it did happen, doing what I had to do."

In 2000, with less than four years on the job, he'd done the normal rotations through 14 Division, one of Toronto's busiest, with the gamut of calls that ranged from him ending up reading "an old lady's mail for her and discovering that her son was embezzling" to attending armed robberies to investigating property crimes and going to community meetings.

On the night in question, he and Det.-Const. Lemaitre got a simple call for an "unwanted guest" at the 7-Eleven store and were told a man who'd been in a fight was now refusing to leave, making the clerks so uneasy one of them had phoned 911.

That was the sum total of what the young officers knew about Mr. Vass, and nothing about him, at first, particularly alarmed them: On the store videotape, wearing shorts and black socks, he appears harmless, relaxed and easy.

But Mr. Vass, through no fault of his own, was ill. He'd suffered from either schizophrenia or bipolar disorder (the diagnosis varied) most of his adult life, and was frequently dangerously violent when in the worst grips of the illness - attacking medical staff or police, once setting fire to an inhabited house, and doing all this on a dime, with a split-second change.

If his violence was atypical of the mentally ill, Mr. Vass's pattern was otherwise too familiar: He'd do well while on his meds, then come to believe he didn't need them or to loathe the side effects more than he appreciated the benefits, yank himself off them, and then spin out of control. It is a tragic bloody cycle, with help hard to come by, and police often alone on the front line.

It was at the end of his cross-examination by Mr. Rosenthal that the depth of Det.-Const. Duncan's regret became clear. The lawyer had been asking if he would do anything differently had he known Mr. Vass was going to die.

"I truly believe what I did was right," he said. "I, probably more than 99 per cent of people on this job, empathize with people with mental health issues.... I wish I'd known about his past. I wish I'd known Mr. Vass had been violent and that his mental history was on the computer that night. I wish I'd had a way to keep him on his meds.... If I knew he was mentally ill and had tried to kill people in the past, burned people.... He was a nice guy, it's not his fault he suffered from this disease."
Later, Anita Szigeti, who represents the Empowerment Council, a group of mental health survivors and consumers, briefly questioned the officer.

He'd had a chance to look over her potential proposed recommendations, which at some point will become public. He agreed with them all, and had one of his own - a sort of giant MedicAlert mental health bracelet, available to police officers, of what Phil Duncan called a do-and-don't list, words that might set the person off or upset him, approaches that hadn't worked in the past.
In about 10 minutes, Ms. Szigeti accomplished more than Mr. Rosenthal did in about three hours, and for my money, revealed more truth.
